questions.solution:
$1\ \text{nm} = \mathbf{10^{-9}\ \text{m}}$, a billionth of a metre.

Nanoscience deals with structures between about **1 and 100 nm**. For scale, a hydrogen atom is about $0.1\ \text{nm}$ across and a DNA double helix about $2\ \text{nm}$ wide.

The lower bound is roughly atomic size; the upper bound is where the special properties of the nanoscale fade into ordinary bulk behaviour.

questions.q: Nanomaterials differ markedly from the same substance in bulk chiefly because of:
options: A very large surface area to volume ratio and quantum confinement
questions.solution:
Two effects act together.

**Surface area to volume ratio** becomes enormous as particles shrink, so a far greater fraction of atoms lies on the surface — and surface atoms are more reactive. This is why nanoparticle catalysts are so effective.

**Quantum confinement**: when a particle becomes comparable in size to the electron wavelength, the energy levels become discrete and size-dependent. The band gap widens as the particle shrinks.

The composition is unchanged throughout — gold nanoparticles are still gold, yet they appear red rather than golden and melt hundreds of degrees below bulk gold.

options: Cylindrical structures of rolled-up graphene sheets
questions.solution:
A carbon nanotube is a **rolled-up sheet of graphene** forming a seamless cylinder, typically a few nanometres across and up to millimetres long.

They have extraordinary properties: tensile strength around **100 times that of steel at one sixth the weight**, excellent thermal conductivity, and electrical behaviour that is either **metallic or semiconducting depending on how the sheet is rolled** — the chirality.

**Fullerene** ($\text{C}_{60}$) is the spherical form, the buckyball.

questions.q: The degrees of freedom of a robotic arm refers to:
options: The number of independent movements it can make
questions.solution:
**Degrees of freedom** is the number of **independent movements** a robot can perform, each usually corresponding to one joint.

A rigid body in three-dimensional space has **six** degrees of freedom — three translations and three rotations — so an arm needs at least six to place an object at any position **and** in any orientation.

More than six gives redundancy, which allows the arm to reach round obstacles; the human arm has seven for this reason.

questions.q: In a robot, the component that provides motion is the:
questions.solution:
The **actuator** converts energy into motion — an electric motor, or a hydraulic or pneumatic cylinder. It is the robot's muscle.

The **sensor** gathers information about the environment, the robot's senses. The **controller** is the computer that processes that information and commands the actuators, the brain.

A robot needs all four, and the **feedback loop** from sensor to controller to actuator is what distinguishes a robot from a merely automatic machine.

questions.q: Gold nanoparticles appear red rather than golden because of:
options: Surface plasmon resonance at the nanoscale
questions.solution:
**Surface plasmon resonance**: the conduction electrons in the nanoparticle oscillate collectively at a frequency that depends on the particle's **size and shape**, absorbing light strongly at that frequency.

For gold particles of a few tens of nanometres this absorption falls in the green, so the transmitted light appears **red**.

The effect was used long before it was understood — medieval stained glass gets its ruby colour from exactly this, and the Lycurgus Cup in the British Museum changes colour with the lighting for the same reason.

questions.q: The alloys used for muscle wires in Robots are :
questions.solution: Muscle wires are **shape memory alloys** such as nitinol (nickel–titanium). Heated by a current they return to a remembered shape and contract, working like a muscle.

questions.q: The gravitational waves were theoretically proposed by :
questions.solution: **Albert Einstein** predicted gravitational waves in 1916 from his general theory of relativity. LIGO first detected them in 2015, from two merging black holes.

questions.q: “Ski wax” is an application of nano product in the field of :
questions.solution: Nano ski wax gives a smoother, harder, water-repelling glide surface: an application in **sports**.

questions.q: By what factor does the surface area to volume ratio increase when a sphere's radius is reduced from $1000\ \text{nm}$ to $10\ \text{nm}$?
questions.solution:
For a sphere, $\dfrac{\text{surface area}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{4\pi r^{2}}{\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}} = \dfrac{3}{r}$.

So the ratio is **inversely proportional to the radius**.

Reducing $r$ by a factor of $\dfrac{1000}{10} = 100$ increases the ratio by a factor of $\mathbf{100}$.

This single fact is most of why nanomaterials behave differently: a hundred times more of the material is at the surface, where the chemistry happens.

questions.q: How many nanometres are there in one micrometre?
How many degrees of freedom does a rigid body have in three-dimensional space?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{6}$ — three **translations** along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes, and three **rotations** about them (roll, pitch and yaw).

This is why a robotic arm needs at least six joints to place an object at any position **and** in any orientation. Fewer, and some orientations are unreachable.

questions.q: Nanomaterials are conventionally defined as having at least one dimension smaller than how many nanometres?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{100\ \text{nm}}$ is the conventional upper limit.

Above it, the surface-to-volume ratio and quantum confinement effects become too weak to distinguish the material from the bulk. The boundary is a convention rather than a sharp physical threshold, but it is where the special behaviour fades.

questions.q: How many carbon atoms are there in a buckminsterfullerene molecule?
questions.solution:
$\mathbf{60}$ carbon atoms, hence $\text{C}_{60}$.

They are arranged in 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons — exactly the pattern of a football. It is named after Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes have the same structure, and its discovery won the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by nanoscience and nanotechnology. Describe why materials behave differently at the nanoscale, outline the two approaches to nanofabrication, and discuss both applications and concerns.
questions.solution:
**Definitions.** **Nanoscience** is the study of structures and phenomena at the nanoscale, conventionally **1 to 100 nm** in at least one dimension. **Nanotechnology** is the application of that understanding to make useful devices and materials.

For scale: a hydrogen atom is about $0.1\ \text{nm}$, a DNA helix $2\ \text{nm}$ wide, a virus $100\ \text{nm}$, and a human hair about $80{,}000\ \text{nm}$ thick.

**Why behaviour changes at the nanoscale.** This is the heart of the subject, and there are two distinct reasons.

**1. Surface area to volume ratio.** For a sphere this ratio is $\dfrac{3}{r}$ — **inversely proportional to the radius**. Shrinking a particle a hundredfold increases the ratio a hundredfold.

A far greater fraction of the atoms therefore sits at the **surface**, where bonds are unsatisfied and reactivity is high. A 3 nm particle has roughly half its atoms on the surface; a bulk crystal has essentially none.

This explains why nanoparticle catalysts work so well, why nanoscale aluminium is used in rocket propellant while a block of aluminium is inert, and why melting points drop — a surface atom is less strongly held than one in the interior, so a particle mostly made of surface melts more easily. Gold melts at $1064^\circ\text{C}$ in bulk and near $300^\circ\text{C}$ at a few nanometres.

**2. Quantum confinement.** When a particle's size approaches the electron's wavelength, the electron is confined in a box small enough for quantum mechanics to dominate. Its energy levels become **discrete** and depend on the box size, so the **band gap widens as the particle shrinks**.

The consequence is striking: **optical properties become tunable by size alone**. Quantum dots of the same material fluoresce at different colours depending only on their diameter — used in displays and in biological imaging.

Gold nanoparticles appear **red** rather than golden through the related effect of surface plasmon resonance, where the conduction electrons oscillate collectively at a size-dependent frequency.

**The crucial point** is that in both cases the **chemical composition is unchanged**. Gold nanoparticles are still gold. The properties change because of **size**, which is a genuinely new idea — classically, a material's properties do not depend on how much of it there is.

**Two approaches to fabrication.**

**Top-down** starts with bulk material and removes from it: photolithography, electron-beam lithography, ball milling. It is the established route of the semiconductor industry and is well controlled, but it is **limited by the resolution of the tools** and is wasteful, since most of the material is discarded.

**Bottom-up** builds structures **from atoms and molecules upward**: chemical vapour deposition, sol-gel methods, molecular self-assembly. It offers finer control, less waste and the possibility of structures top-down cannot reach, but controlling self-assembly is difficult and it does not yet scale as readily.

Feynman anticipated the bottom-up idea in 1959 in **There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom**, decades before any means of doing it existed.

**Applications.**

**Medicine** — targeted drug delivery, where a nanocarrier releases its drug only at a tumour, sparing healthy tissue; contrast agents for imaging; nanoparticle-based diagnostics.

**Electronics** — transistors now have features of a few nanometres, and carbon nanotubes and graphene are candidates to succeed silicon.

**Energy** — higher-capacity batteries, more efficient solar cells, better fuel-cell catalysts.

**Materials** — nanotube composites of great strength and low weight, scratch-resistant coatings, self-cleaning and water-repellent surfaces.

**Environment** — water purification membranes, and nanoparticles for remediating contaminated soil.

**Concerns, which deserve to be stated honestly.**

**Toxicity.** The very properties that make nanoparticles useful — small size, high reactivity, large surface area — also let them **cross biological barriers** that stop larger particles: deep into the lungs, potentially the blood-brain barrier. **A material safe in bulk is not automatically safe at the nanoscale**, and long-term effects are not yet well characterised.

**Environmental persistence.** Nanoparticles released into water or soil may accumulate through food chains in ways not yet understood.

**Regulation.** Legal frameworks lag behind the technology, and products containing nanomaterials have reached the market ahead of settled safety standards.

**Ethical and social questions.** Military uses, surveillance made possible by very small sensors, and the risk that the benefits accrue only to wealthy countries.

**The balanced position** is that nanotechnology is genuinely transformative and that its risks are real but largely **unquantified rather than demonstrated**. The responsible course is to develop the technology and the toxicology together, which is why nanotoxicology has grown up alongside it — and it is a better response than either uncritical enthusiasm or refusal.
